blocks.body:
A school must schedule exams so that no student has two exams at the same time. Draw a graph (see [[graph-basics]]) with a vertex for each exam and an edge between two exams that share a student. A schedule with $k$ time slots is a way to give each vertex one of $k$ labels so that adjacent vertices get different labels. The fewest slots possible is the chromatic number of the graph.

The same model covers radio frequencies for interfering transmitters, registers for variables in a compiler, and colours for countries on a map. This lesson develops the basic upper and lower bounds for the chromatic number, proves when two colours suffice, and surveys the landmarks: Brooks' theorem, the four colour theorem and Hadwiger's conjecture.

blocks.title: Proper colouring and chromatic number
blocks.body:
A proper $k$-colouring of a graph $G = (V,E)$ is a map $c : V \to \{1, \dots, k\}$ with $c(u) \ne c(v)$ for every edge $uv$. The chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is the least $k$ for which a proper $k$-colouring exists.

Each colour class $c^{-1}(i)$ is an independent set (no two of its vertices are adjacent), so a proper $k$-colouring is the same thing as a partition of $V$ into $k$ independent sets.

blocks.title: First examples and lower bounds
blocks.body:
The complete graph $K_n$ needs $n$ colours, since all vertices are mutually adjacent. A cycle $C_n$ needs $2$ colours if $n$ is even (alternate) and $3$ if $n$ is odd: going round the cycle with two colours forces them to alternate, which fails to close up after an odd number of steps.

Two lower bounds come straight from the definition. Write $\omega(G)$ for the size of the largest clique (set of mutually adjacent vertices) and $\alpha(G)$ for the size of the largest independent set. A clique needs distinct colours, so $\chi(G) \ge \omega(G)$. And in a proper colouring with $\chi(G)$ colours each colour class has at most $\alpha(G)$ vertices, so $|V| \le \chi(G)\,\alpha(G)$, that is
$$\chi(G) \ge \frac{|V|}{\alpha(G)}.$$
The second bound can be much better than the first. For $C_5$ we have $\omega = 2$, but $\alpha = 2$ gives $\chi \ge 5/2$, so $\chi(C_5) \ge 3$.

blocks.title: Two-colourable graphs
blocks.body: A graph satisfies $\chi(G) \le 2$ (it is bipartite) if and only if it contains no cycle of odd length.

In a proper $2$-colouring the colours alternate along any cycle, so a cycle returns to its starting colour only after an even number of steps. Hence a bipartite graph has no odd cycle.

Conversely, suppose there is no odd cycle. It suffices to colour each connected component. Fix a vertex $r$ in the component, and colour each vertex $v$ by the parity of its distance $d(v)$ from $r$. Suppose some edge $uv$ had $d(u) \equiv d(v) \pmod 2$. A shortest path from $r$ to $u$, the edge $uv$, and a shortest path from $v$ back to $r$ form a closed walk of odd length $d(u) + 1 + d(v)$.

An odd closed walk always contains an odd cycle. Induct on its length: if no vertex repeats (apart from the start, which is also the end), it is itself a cycle, of length at least $3$ since its length is odd and a closed walk of length $1$ is impossible in a graph without loops. If some vertex repeats, split the walk at the repeat into two shorter closed walks whose lengths add to an odd number; one of them is odd, and induction applies. This contradicts the assumption, so the parity colouring is proper.

blocks.title: Greedy bound
blocks.body: For every graph, $\chi(G) \le \Delta(G) + 1$, where $\Delta(G)$ is the maximum degree. More generally, if every non-empty subgraph of $G$ has a vertex of degree at most $d$, then $\chi(G) \le d + 1$.

Order the vertices $v_1, \dots, v_n$ and colour them in this order, giving each the smallest colour not used by its already coloured neighbours. A vertex with at most $d$ earlier neighbours finds a free colour among $\{1, \dots, d+1\}$. If $d = \Delta(G)$, every vertex has at most $d$ neighbours at all, which proves the first statement.

For the second, choose the order cleverly. Let $v_n$ be a vertex of degree at most $d$ in $G$, let $v_{n-1}$ be a vertex of degree at most $d$ in $G - v_n$, and so on, always removing a vertex of degree at most $d$ in what remains. Then each $v_i$ has at most $d$ neighbours among $v_1, \dots, v_{i-1}$, and the greedy colouring in the order $v_1, \dots, v_n$ uses at most $d + 1$ colours.

blocks.title: Brooks' theorem and planar graphs
blocks.body:
When is $\Delta + 1$ colours actually needed? Complete graphs ($\chi(K_n) = n = \Delta + 1$) and odd cycles ($\chi = 3 = \Delta + 1$) need them. Brooks (1941) proved these are the only connected examples: if $G$ is connected and is neither a complete graph nor an odd cycle, then $\chi(G) \le \Delta(G)$. The proof is a careful choice of greedy order and we omit it.

A graph is planar if it can be drawn in the plane without crossing edges. From Euler's formula for plane drawings one gets that a simple planar graph with $n \ge 3$ vertices has at most $3n - 6$ edges. Every subgraph of a planar graph is planar, and the average degree is then less than $6$, so every non-empty subgraph has a vertex of degree at most $5$. By the greedy bound, $\chi(G) \le 6$ for every planar graph. A cleverer recolouring argument (Heawood, 1890, repairing Kempe's flawed attempt) gives $5$. The four colour theorem, that $4$ colours always suffice, was proved by Appel and Haken in 1976 with a computer check of a large set of configurations. A simpler, still computer-assisted proof by Robertson, Sanders, Seymour and Thomas followed in 1997, and the proof was later formally verified by Gonthier using the Coq proof assistant.

blocks.title: Large chromatic number without large cliques
blocks.body:
One might think a graph needs many colours only because it contains a large clique. This is false. Mycielski (1955) gave a construction that turns a triangle-free graph $G$ with $\chi(G) = k$ into a triangle-free graph $M(G)$ with $\chi(M(G)) = k + 1$. Take the vertices $v_1, \dots, v_n$ of $G$, new vertices $u_1, \dots, u_n$ and one more vertex $w$. Keep the edges of $G$, join $u_i$ to every $v_j$ that is adjacent to $v_i$, and join $w$ to every $u_i$.

Starting from $C_5$ gives the Grötzsch graph with $11$ vertices and $20$ edges: triangle-free, with chromatic number $4$. Iterating gives triangle-free graphs of every chromatic number. Erdős (1959) proved much more with the [[probabilistic-method]]: for all $g$ and $k$ there are graphs with no cycles of length less than $g$ and chromatic number greater than $k$. So the chromatic number is a global property that cannot be detected by looking at small pieces of the graph.

blocks.title: Hadwiger's conjecture
blocks.body: A minor of $G$ is a graph obtained from a subgraph of $G$ by contracting edges (merging the two ends of an edge into one vertex). Hadwiger conjectured in 1943 that every graph with $\chi(G) \ge t$ has the complete graph $K_t$ as a minor. For $t \le 4$ this is not hard. For $t = 5$, Wagner showed in 1937 that the statement is equivalent to the four colour theorem, so it holds by Appel and Haken's work, and Robertson, Seymour and Thomas proved the case $t = 6$ in 1993, again by reducing it to the four colour theorem. For $t \ge 7$ it is open.

blocks.title: The Petersen graph
blocks.body: The Petersen graph has vertices $0, \dots, 9$; the outer vertices $0, \dots, 4$ form a $5$-cycle, the inner vertices $5, \dots, 9$ are joined as $5\text{–}7\text{–}9\text{–}6\text{–}8\text{–}5$, and each $i \le 4$ is joined to $i + 5$. Find its chromatic number.
blocks.solution:
The graph is $3$-regular, connected, not complete (it has $10$ vertices but degree $3$) and not a cycle. Brooks' theorem gives $\chi \le \Delta = 3$. The outer $5$-cycle is an odd cycle, so $\chi \ge 3$. Hence $\chi = 3$.

Without Brooks one can simply exhibit a colouring. Colour the outer cycle $0, 1, 2, 3, 4$ with $1, 2, 1, 2, 3$. Each inner vertex $i + 5$ must avoid the colour of $i$ and of its two inner neighbours; for instance inner colours $2, 1, 3, 3, 2$ for vertices $5, 6, 7, 8, 9$ work, as one checks edge by edge.

blocks.title: Colouring a cycle
blocks.body:
Let $P_k(G)$ be the number of proper colourings of $G$ using colours from $\{1, \dots, k\}$ (not all colours need be used). Show that for $n \ge 3$
$$P_k(C_n) = (k-1)^n + (-1)^n (k-1).$$
blocks.solution:
For a path on $n$ vertices, colour the vertices from one end: $k$ choices for the first and $k - 1$ for each later one, so there are $k(k-1)^{n-1}$ colourings.

Number the vertices of $C_n$ as $1, \dots, n$ around the cycle and remove the edge between $n$ and $1$; this leaves a path. Its proper colourings split into two kinds: those with $c(1) \ne c(n)$, which are exactly the proper colourings of $C_n$, and those with $c(1) = c(n)$. For $n \ge 4$ the second kind correspond one-to-one to proper colourings of $C_{n-1}$: delete vertex $n$ and join $n-1$ to $1$. The path's condition $c(n-1) \ne c(n) = c(1)$ becomes exactly the condition on the new edge between $n-1$ and $1$, and since $n - 1 \ge 3$ the result is a genuine cycle on $n-1$ vertices. Conversely, a proper colouring of $C_{n-1}$ extends uniquely by giving vertex $n$ the colour of vertex $1$. So
$$P_k(C_n) = k(k-1)^{n-1} - P_k(C_{n-1}) \qquad (n \ge 4).$$
For $n = 3$ the formula gives $(k-1)^3 - (k-1) = (k-1)(k-2)k$, which is right: colour the triangle's vertices in turn with $k$, $k-1$, $k-2$ choices. If the formula holds for $n - 1$, then
$$k(k-1)^{n-1} - \big[(k-1)^{n-1} + (-1)^{n-1}(k-1)\big] = (k-1)^{n-1}(k - 1) + (-1)^n (k-1),$$
which is the formula for $n$. With $k = 3$ and $n = 5$: $32 - 2 = 30$ proper $3$-colourings of $C_5$.

blocks.title: Many colours need many edges
blocks.body: Show that a graph with $m$ edges satisfies $\binom{\chi(G)}{2} \le m$, and hence $\chi(G) \le \frac12 + \sqrt{2m + \frac14}$.
blocks.solution:
Take a proper colouring with $\chi = \chi(G)$ colours. For any two colours $i \ne j$ there must be an edge between the classes of $i$ and of $j$: otherwise the union of the two classes would be independent and we could recolour it with one colour, getting a proper colouring with $\chi - 1$ colours. Different pairs of colours give different edges, so $m \ge \binom{\chi}{2}$.

Then $\chi^2 - \chi - 2m \le 0$, and since $\chi$ is at most the positive root, $\chi \le \frac{1 + \sqrt{1 + 8m}}{2} = \frac12 + \sqrt{2m + \frac14}$. Equality holds for complete graphs, since $K_n$ has $\binom n2$ edges.

blocks.body:
- $\chi(G) \ge \omega(G)$ can be far from equality: the Grötzsch graph has $\omega = 2$ and $\chi = 4$.
- The greedy algorithm depends heavily on the order. On $K_{m,m}$ with a perfect matching removed (vertices $a_i, b_i$, with $a_i b_j$ an edge exactly when $i \ne j$), the order $a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2, \dots$ makes greedy use $m$ colours, although the graph is bipartite.
- The four colour theorem is about planar graphs. $K_5$ needs $5$ colours; it is simply not planar.
- $P_k(G)$ counts colourings with colours from a set of size $k$, not colourings that use exactly $k$ colours.

Colouring the edges of a complete graph instead of its vertices leads to [[ramsey]] theory; colouring hyperedges leads to the property B problems of [[hypergraphs]]. The chromatic number of a forbidden graph $H$ controls how many edges a graph can have without containing $H$, by the Erdős–Stone theorem in [[extremal-graphs]]. Edge colourings of bipartite graphs come from repeated perfect matchings, as in [[cycles-matchings]].

Deciding whether a graph is $3$-colourable is NP-complete (see [[p-vs-np]]), even though $2$-colourability is easy by the odd-cycle theorem. In [[discrete-geometry]], the chromatic number of the plane (points at distance $1$ adjacent) is known to lie between $5$ and $7$; the lower bound $5$ was proved by de Grey in 2018, improving the classical bound $4$.

1. Show that $\chi(G) + \chi(\overline G) \le n + 1$ for every graph $G$ on $n$ vertices, where $\overline G$ is the complement.
2. Prove that Mycielski's construction keeps graphs triangle-free.
3. Find the chromatic number of the graph whose vertices are $1, \dots, 20$, with $a$ and $b$ adjacent when one divides the other.
4. Show that for every graph $G$ some ordering of the vertices makes the greedy algorithm use exactly $\chi(G)$ colours.

sources.ref: Appel & Haken, Every planar map is four colorable, Illinois Journal of Mathematics (1977)
